## STEP 3: MASTER HIERARCHICAL CHART

## 1. Microsoft Entra ID (Identity Management)

### S - Simple Core
Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is Microsoft's cloud-based identity service that controls who can access your Azure resources and what they can do with them.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2023, a Fortune 500 retailer suffered a $4.2M data breach when an ex-employee's Entra ID account wasn't properly deactivated after termination, allowing 8 months of unauthorized access to customer databases - highlighting why centralized identity lifecycle management through Entra ID's automatic deprovisioning features is now mandated in their security baseline.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Entra ID like an airport security checkpoint system: The airport (Azure) has multiple terminals (subscriptions), but everyone goes through the same TSA checkpoint (Entra ID) first. Your boarding pass (user account) shows which terminals you can access, your ID verification (authentication) proves who you are, and your TSA PreCheck status (assigned roles) determines what you can carry through. Just like TSA keeps a single database for all airlines, Entra ID maintains one identity source for all Azure services.

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** When should you use Entra ID instead of on-premises Active Directory for Azure access?
**Answer:** Always use Entra ID as the primary identity provider for Azure resources - even if you have on-premises AD, sync it to Entra ID using Azure AD Connect to enable cloud authentication and conditional access policies for Azure portal access.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Microsoft Entra ID** with **Microsoft Entra Domain Services**: Entra ID provides cloud-native identity and OAuth/SAML authentication for modern apps, while Entra Domain Services provides domain join, LDAP, and Kerberos for legacy applications that require traditional domain controller protocols.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Azure subscription with Global Administrator or at least User Administrator role in the tenant
  • Selection: Entra ID Free (included with Azure subscription), Entra ID Premium P1 ($6/user/month - adds Conditional Access), or Entra ID Premium P2 ($9/user/month - adds Identity Protection and PIM)
  • Execution: Navigate to Azure Portal > Microsoft Entra ID > Overview blade > Tenant properties to verify tenant creation and custom domain setup

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Add custom domain name: Entra ID > Custom domain names > Add custom domain > Verify ownership via TXT or MX DNS record (e.g., MS=ms12345678 in contoso.com DNS)
  • Set primary domain: Custom domain names > Select domain > Make primary (changes default @contoso.com suffix for new users)
  • Enable Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR): Password reset > Properties > Self-service password reset enabled = Selected > Choose security group
  • Configure authentication methods: SSPR > Authentication methods > Minimum of 2 required (options: Mobile app notification, Mobile app code, Email, Mobile phone, Office phone, Security questions)
  • Set up Conditional Access: Security > Conditional Access > New policy > Assignments (Users, Cloud apps) > Conditions (Sign-in risk, Device platforms) > Access controls (Require MFA, Require compliant device)
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** Conditional Access (Premium P1) applies policies at sign-in based on signals, while Identity Protection (Premium P2) uses ML to detect risky sign-ins and risky users automatically
  • **[Design Boundary]:** Entra ID Free tier limits you to 50,000 objects (users + groups + devices), requires upgrade to Premium for unlimited objects and advanced features like dynamic groups or Privileged Identity Management
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests ability to configure custom domains (TXT record verification), enable SSPR with authentication methods, and apply Conditional Access policies requiring MFA for specific user groups or cloud apps

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Entra ID > Sign-in logs (tracks user authentication attempts) and Audit logs (tracks configuration changes like role assignments)
  • Metric: Failed sign-in attempts (filter by Status = Failure, analyze Error code like 50126 for invalid credentials or 530003 for blocked by Conditional Access)
  • Success: Zero authentication errors for test users, custom domain shows "Verified" status, SSPR test completes successfully with 2 authentication methods

## 2. Users and Groups

### S - Simple Core
Users are individual identities (people or service principals) that sign into Azure, while groups are collections of users that you assign permissions to all at once instead of individually.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2022, Capital One was fined $80M partly because individual user accounts had excessive privileges - had they used Entra ID dynamic groups with attribute-based membership (department=Finance), the automatic deprovisioning when employees changed departments would have prevented 23 instances of unauthorized access that auditors discovered during compliance review.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of users and groups like a corporate email distribution system: Individual users are like email addresses (john@company.com), security groups are like distribution lists that don't change often (FinanceTeam@company.com - you manually add/remove members), Microsoft 365 groups are like Teams channels (project-alpha@company.com - comes with shared mailbox and files), and dynamic groups are like auto-populated lists based on job title in HR system (everyone with title=Manager automatically included). When you need to give 50 people access to a storage account, you don't grant 50 individual permissions - you add them to one group and grant the group access.

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** When should you use a security group versus a Microsoft 365 group in Entra ID?
**Answer:** Use security groups for access control to Azure resources (they can be assigned RBAC roles), and Microsoft 365 groups when users also need collaboration features like shared mailbox, SharePoint site, and Teams channel - note that only security groups support dynamic membership based on user attributes.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Member users** with **Guest users (B2B)**: Members are internal employees from your tenant (user@contoso.com) with full directory access, while guests are external identities (partner@fabrikam.com) invited for collaboration with restricted directory permissions and can't read other users by default.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: User Administrator, Groups Administrator, or Global Administrator role in Entra ID (read-only roles can't create users)
  • Selection: Cloud-only user (created directly in Entra ID), Synchronized user (synced from on-premises AD via Azure AD Connect), or Guest user (B2B invitation to external identity)
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Entra ID > Users > New user > Create user (manually) OR Bulk operations > Bulk create (upload CSV with UserPrincipalName, DisplayName, MailNickname columns)

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Create cloud user: Users > New user > User principal name = john@contoso.com, Display name = John Smith, Auto-generate password (check box) > Create
  • Create security group: Entra ID > Groups > New group > Group type = Security, Membership type = Assigned (manual) or Dynamic User (rule-based)
  • Configure dynamic group rule: Membership type = Dynamic User > Add dynamic query > Rule syntax: `(user.department -eq "Finance") -and (user.accountEnabled -eq true)` for automated membership
  • Bulk create users via CSV: Users > Bulk operations > Bulk create > Download CSV template > Fill columns (userPrincipalName, displayName, mailNickname, accountEnabled=true) > Upload
  • Add user to group: Groups > Select group > Members > Add members > Search and select users > Select
  • Invite guest user (B2B): Users > New user > Invite external user > Email = partner@external.com > Personal message = "Join our project workspace" > Invite
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** Assigned groups require manual member management (add/remove users explicitly), while dynamic groups use membership rules that auto-update based on user attributes - dynamic groups require Entra ID Premium P1 license
  • **[Design Boundary]:** Dynamic group membership rules process every 24 hours by default (not real-time), can take up to 1 hour for large tenants, and you cannot combine dynamic user membership with dynamic device membership in same group
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests CSV bulk user creation format, dynamic group rule syntax using user.department and user.jobTitle attributes, and understanding that guest users need redemption (must accept invitation) before gaining access

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Entra ID > Groups > Select group > Members blade (verify dynamic membership count), and Users > Select user > Assigned roles + Group memberships blades
  • Metric: Dynamic group processing state (check Properties > Membership processing status = Complete), guest user RedemptionStatus = Accepted (not PendingAcceptance)
  • Success: Dynamic group member count matches expected users meeting rule criteria, bulk user CSV import shows 0 errors in Results blade, guest users appear in sign-in logs with successful authentication

## 3. Administrative Units

### S - Simple Core
Administrative Units are containers within Entra ID that let you delegate admin permissions to only a subset of users or groups instead of giving someone admin access across your entire directory.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2021, a global manufacturing company with 85,000 employees used Administrative Units to delegate password reset permissions to regional IT teams - the EMEA team could only reset passwords for the 24,000 European users, preventing a security incident when a compromised EMEA admin account couldn't access or modify the 61,000 North American and Asia-Pacific user accounts.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Administrative Units like hospital departments with floor supervisors: The hospital (Entra ID tenant) has a Chief Medical Officer (Global Administrator) who controls everything, but each floor (Administrative Unit) has a supervisor (scoped administrator) who can only manage patients (users) and equipment (resources) on their floor. The ICU supervisor can reset patient codes for ICU rooms but can't touch the Cardiology floor. Without AUs, every supervisor would need full hospital access, which violates principle of least privilege.

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** When should you implement Administrative Units instead of just using regular RBAC roles?
**Answer:** When you need to delegate user management (password resets, profile updates) to regional admins or department heads but don't want them to see or modify users outside their scope - RBAC roles grant permissions to Azure resources, while AUs scope identity management permissions within Entra ID itself.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Administrative Units** with **Management Groups**: Administrative Units scope identity administration within Entra ID (who can manage which users), while Management Groups scope resource administration across Azure subscriptions (which subscriptions inherit which policies) - completely different hierarchy systems.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Entra ID Premium P1 or P2 license (Administrative Units not available in Free tier), Privileged Role Administrator or Global Administrator role required to create AUs
  • Selection: Assigned membership (manually add users/groups to AU) or Dynamic membership (rule-based user assignment using attributes like user.country or user.department) - dynamic requires Premium P1
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Entra ID > Administrative units > Add (or use PowerShell: `New-AzureADMSAdministrativeUnit -DisplayName "EMEA Users"`)

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Create Administrative Unit: Entra ID > Administrative units > Add > Name = "North America Region", Description = "Users in US and Canada offices"
  • Add members manually: Select AU > Users > Add member > Search for users > Select (or add groups if managing group membership)
  • Create dynamic AU: Add > Membership type = Dynamic > Dynamic membership rules > Rule syntax: `(user.country -eq "United States") -or (user.country -eq "Canada")`
  • Assign scoped role: Select AU > Roles and administrators > Add assignment > Select role (e.g., Password Administrator, User Administrator) > Select members > Assign
  • Scope restrictions: Password Administrator scoped to AU can only reset passwords for users in that AU, cannot create new users or modify user attributes outside password reset
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** Helpdesk Administrator role scoped to an AU can reset passwords and invalidate refresh tokens, while User Administrator scoped to AU can additionally update user profiles, manage licenses, and create/delete users within that AU only
  • **[Design Boundary]:** Administrative Units can contain users and groups, but scoped administrators can only manage users within the AU - they cannot manage group memberships or create groups, and dynamic AUs update every 24 hours (not real-time)
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests understanding that scoped roles in AUs require Premium P1, dynamic AU rule syntax using user.country or user.department, and knowing which admin roles can be scoped (Password Administrator, User Administrator) versus which cannot (Global Administrator, Security Administrator)

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Entra ID > Administrative units > Select AU > Users blade (verify member count), and Roles and administrators blade (verify scoped role assignments)
  • Metric: Dynamic AU processing status under Properties > Membership type = Dynamic > Rule processing status = Complete, member count matches expected users meeting criteria
  • Success: Scoped administrator can successfully reset password for user in their AU via Entra ID > Users > Select user > Reset password, but receives "Access Denied" error when attempting same action on user outside their AU

## 4. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

### S - Simple Core
RBAC controls what actions people can perform on Azure resources by assigning roles (collections of permissions) to users, groups, or applications at specific scopes like subscriptions, resource groups, or individual resources.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2019, Tesla's AWS infrastructure was compromised costing $6M because an admin account had unrestricted permissions - implementing proper RBAC with Azure's principle of least privilege (developers get Contributor role on dev resource groups only, not production) prevents similar breaches by limiting blast radius when credentials are compromised.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of RBAC like a corporate building access badge system: The badge (role assignment) gives you specific access levels (permissions like "Owner" = full access, "Contributor" = modify but not grant access, "Reader" = view only) to certain floors (scope: subscription/resource group/resource). A developer's badge might grant Contributor access to the 3rd floor dev lab (dev resource group) but only Reader access to the 10th floor production datacenter (production resource group). The security system (Azure Resource Manager) checks your badge every time you swipe (attempt an action) and allows/denies based on role definition at that scope.

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** If a user has Reader role on subscription level but Contributor role on a specific resource group, what can they do?
**Answer:** They can view everything in the subscription (Reader inherited), but modify resources only in that specific resource group (Contributor overrides at narrower scope) - RBAC combines allow permissions from all assignments, most permissive wins per scope.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Entra ID roles** with **Azure RBAC roles**: Entra ID roles (User Administrator, Global Administrator) manage identities and tenant settings within Entra ID, while Azure RBAC roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader) manage access to Azure resources like VMs and storage accounts - they're separate permission systems.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Owner or User Access Administrator role at the scope where you want to grant access (can't assign roles you don't have permission to assign)
  • Selection: Built-in roles (70+ predefined like Owner, Contributor, Reader, Virtual Machine Contributor) or Custom roles (create specific permission sets) - identify principle of least privilege first
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Subscription/Resource Group/Resource > Access control (IAM) > Add > Add role assignment (or use PowerShell: `New-AzRoleAssignment`)

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Assign built-in role: Resource group > Access control (IAM) > Add role assignment > Role tab > Select "Contributor" > Next > Members tab > Select members > Assign user or group
  • Grant VM-specific access: Virtual machine resource > Access control (IAM) > Add > "Virtual Machine Contributor" role (can start/stop/restart VMs but not modify network or storage) > Assign to user
  • Subscription-level assignment: Subscription > IAM > Add > Owner role (full access including grant access to others), Contributor (manage resources but not grant access), or Reader (view only) > Assign to group for inheritance
  • Deny assignments: IAM > Check Access > Deny assignments tab (created by Azure Blueprints or Managed Applications to prevent specific actions even if role grants permission) - read-only, cannot be manually created
  • Check effective permissions: IAM > Check access > Select user > View role assignments > Shows inherited assignments from subscription/management group levels plus direct assignments
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** Owner role includes `*/write` (modify resources) AND `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write` (grant access to others), while Contributor role includes `*/write` but explicitly denies `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/*` (cannot grant access)
  • **[Design Boundary]:** RBAC assignments take up to 30 minutes to propagate globally (cached at each Azure region), assignments at subscription level inherit to all resource groups and resources (can't block inheritance except with deny assignments), maximum 2,000 role assignments per subscription
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests understanding that Owner can grant access while Contributor cannot, role assignments inherit down the hierarchy (subscription → resource group → resource), and custom roles require `Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions/write` permission to create

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Azure Portal > Subscription/Resource Group > Access control (IAM) > Role assignments tab, or Azure Monitor > Activity log filtered by Category = Administrative + Operation name = "Create role assignment"
  • Metric: Review "Not authorized" errors in Activity log (indicates missing RBAC permissions), check IAM > Check access for specific user to verify effective permissions at scope
  • Success: User can perform intended actions (e.g., Contributor can create VM via Portal successfully), unauthorized actions return "403 Forbidden" error, Activity log shows successful "Create role assignment" operation

## 5. Custom RBAC Roles

### S - Simple Core
Custom RBAC roles let you create specific permission sets tailored to your organization's needs when Azure's 70+ built-in roles are either too broad or too restrictive for a particular job function.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2020, a healthcare provider created a custom "HIPAA Compliance Auditor" role with read-only permissions to audit logs and diagnostic settings but explicitly denied access to patient data - this role saved $2.3M in audit costs by allowing their 15-person compliance team to review security configurations across 4,000 resources without needing expensive Security Administrator licenses or risking PHI exposure from over-privileged access.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of custom RBAC roles like creating a custom job description: Built-in roles are like standard industry job titles (Manager, Developer, Analyst) with predefined responsibilities, but custom roles let you write a specific job description (Database Backup Operator) that picks exactly which tasks (Actions) the person can do (read database, create backups), which tasks they absolutely cannot do (NotActions: delete database, modify credentials), and which data-level operations are allowed (DataActions: read backup blobs). You wouldn't give someone full Manager permissions when they only need backup responsibilities.

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** When should you create a custom role instead of using a built-in role like Contributor or Reader?
**Answer:** Create a custom role when you need to grant specific permissions that built-in roles don't match - for example, allowing database backup operations but denying restore operations, or granting VM start/stop permissions without allowing VM creation/deletion - whenever principle of least privilege requires granular control.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Actions** with **DataActions** in custom roles: Actions control management plane operations like creating VMs or storage accounts (Azure Resource Manager operations), while DataActions control data plane operations like reading blobs or writing to Key Vault secrets - you need both to grant full access to data in storage accounts.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Owner or User Access Administrator role at subscription level (custom roles cannot be created at resource group scope), understanding of Azure Resource Provider operations format (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write)
  • Selection: JSON definition method (Portal editor or ARM template) or PowerShell/CLI (New-AzRoleDefinition cmdlet) - choose based on automation needs and whether you need to deploy across multiple subscriptions
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Subscriptions > Select subscription > Access control (IAM) > Roles > Add > Add custom role (or use Azure CLI: `az role definition create --role-definition role.json`)

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Create custom role via Portal: IAM > Roles > Add custom role > Start from scratch > Basics tab > Role name = "Virtual Machine Operator", Description = "Can start, stop, restart VMs but not create or delete"
  • Add Actions: Permissions tab > Add permissions > Search "Microsoft.Compute" > Select "Virtual Machines" > Check boxes: `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read`, `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action`, `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/restart/action`, `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/powerOff/action`
  • Add NotActions: JSON tab > Edit > Add `"NotActions": ["Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete", "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write"]` to explicitly deny VM creation/deletion/modification
  • Set assignable scopes: Assignable scopes tab > Add subscription or resource group scope (e.g., `/subscriptions/{subscription-id}` or `/subscriptions/{subscription-id}/resourceGroups/production-rg`)
  • Example JSON definition for Storage Blob Reader with data access:
    ```json
    {
      "Name": "Storage Blob Data Reader Custom",
      "Description": "Read blob data but not list keys",
      "Actions": ["Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/read"],
      "NotActions": ["Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action"],
      "DataActions": ["Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/read"],
      "AssignableScopes": ["/subscriptions/{subscription-id}"]
    }
    ```
  • Wildcard usage: Use wildcards carefully - `"Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/*"` grants all VM operations, `"*/read"` grants read on all resources, but wildcards in NotActions create maintenance issues when new actions are added
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** NotActions subtract from Actions (if Actions includes `*` then NotActions can exclude specific operations), but NotActions alone don't grant anything - you must have a corresponding Actions permission first
  • **[Design Boundary]:** Custom roles can be assigned at subscription, resource group, or resource scope (but cannot be created below subscription level), maximum 5,000 custom roles per Entra ID tenant, role definition changes take up to 30 minutes to propagate to all Azure regions
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests JSON structure with Actions/NotActions/DataActions arrays, understanding that AssignableScopes limits where role can be assigned, and recognizing when DataActions are required (blob storage data access) versus when Actions are sufficient (resource management)

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Azure Portal > Subscriptions > IAM > Roles tab > Type = CustomRole filter, or use PowerShell: `Get-AzRoleDefinition | Where-Object {$_.IsCustom -eq $true}`
  • Metric: Check role assignment count for custom role via IAM > Role assignments tab > Filter by role name, verify Actions list includes only intended operations via Roles > Select custom role > JSON view
  • Success: Custom role appears in Add role assignment wizard, user with custom role can perform allowed actions (returns 200 OK in Activity log) and receives 403 Forbidden for operations in NotActions list, no overly broad wildcards like `*/*` in Actions array

## 6. Microsoft Entra Domain Services

### S - Simple Core
Entra Domain Services provides managed domain controllers in Azure that let you join VMs to a domain, use Group Policy, and authenticate with NTLM/Kerberos without running your own domain controller infrastructure.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2021, a financial services company migrated 300 legacy Windows Server 2008 applications to Azure that required domain join and Kerberos authentication - using Entra Domain Services ($109/month) instead of building IaaS domain controllers saved $180K annually in infrastructure costs and 400 admin hours per year, while maintaining the LDAP and Group Policy requirements that these legacy apps needed.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Entra Domain Services like hiring a managed security service for your office building: Instead of hiring, training, and managing your own security guards (building domain controllers on VMs), you contract a professional security company (Microsoft) that provides trained guards (managed DCs) who know your building's access rules (synced from Entra ID). The guards handle ID checks (Kerberos authentication), enforce building policies (Group Policy), and maintain access logs (LDAP queries), but you don't deal with their payroll, training, or shift scheduling (patching, monitoring, HA).

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** When should you use Entra Domain Services instead of deploying domain controllers on Azure VMs?
**Answer:** Use Entra Domain Services when you need domain services (LDAP, Kerberos, domain join, Group Policy) for lift-and-shift applications but don't want to manage domain controller VMs, patching, backups, or replication - ideal for legacy apps that can't use modern authentication but don't need trust relationships with on-premises forests.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Entra Domain Services** with **Entra ID**: Entra ID provides modern OAuth/SAML cloud authentication for SaaS apps, while Entra Domain Services provides traditional domain controller functionality (LDAP, Kerberos, NTLM) for legacy apps - Entra Domain Services is actually a managed AD DS domain that syncs users from Entra ID.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Azure subscription with at least Contributor role, dedicated subnet in VNet (must not contain other resources, minimum /24 CIDR), custom domain name configured in Entra ID (e.g., contoso.com, not default .onmicrosoft.com)
  • Selection: Standard tier (supports up to 25,000 objects, $109/month) or Enterprise tier (supports 100,000 objects, forest trusts, $349/month) - Enterprise required for multi-forest on-premises integration
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Create a resource > Search "Azure AD Domain Services" > Create > Provide domain name (aaddscontoso.com), select VNet and subnet, choose SKU

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Create Entra Domain Services: Create resource > Entra Domain Services > Basics > DNS domain name = aaddscontoso.com (must not conflict with existing domains), SKU = Standard, Region = East US
  • Select network: Networking tab > Virtual network = prod-vnet > Subnet = Create new subnet named "AADDS-Subnet" with address range 10.0.2.0/24 (must be dedicated, no other resources allowed)
  • Configure administrator group: Entra ID > Groups > Create "AAD DC Administrators" security group > Add members who need domain admin privileges (these users become domain admins in managed domain)
  • Wait for deployment: Takes 60-90 minutes to deploy managed domain controllers (two DCs for HA), DNS servers provisioned with IP addresses in AADDS-Subnet
  • Update VNet DNS: After deployment, VNet > DNS servers > Custom > Add two DNS IP addresses from Entra Domain Services Overview blade (e.g., 10.0.2.4, 10.0.2.5) > Save (required for domain join to work)
  • Enable password hash sync: For cloud-only users, forces password change on next sign-in to generate NTLM/Kerberos hashes (these sync to managed domain within 20 minutes); for synced users, enable Password Hash Sync in Azure AD Connect
  • Join VM to domain: On Windows VM > System Properties > Computer Name > Change > Domain = aaddscontoso.com > Enter credentials of user in "AAD DC Administrators" group > Restart VM
  • Create Group Policy: From domain-joined VM > Install RSAT tools > Group Policy Management > Connect to aaddscontoso.com forest > Create GPO linked to "AADDC Computers" OU (default OU for VMs)
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** The "AAD DC Administrators" group grants domain admin rights in the managed domain (can join machines, modify GPOs), while Global Administrator in Entra ID does NOT automatically get domain admin rights - you must explicitly add users to AAD DC Administrators group
  • **[Design Boundary]:** You cannot extend the schema of the managed domain, cannot create custom OUs at root level (only within AADDC Computers or AADDC Users containers), forest trust only supported in Enterprise SKU, and you cannot RDP to the domain controller VMs (fully managed by Microsoft)
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests understanding that VNet DNS servers must be updated to managed domain DNS IPs, password hash sync is required for authentication, AAD DC Administrators group membership required for domain admin tasks, and dedicated subnet requirement

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Azure Portal > Entra Domain Services resource > Health blade (shows replication status, secure LDAP configuration, DNS resolution), Alerts blade (critical: password hash sync issues, DC unavailability)
  • Metric: Domain Controller status (both DCs should show "Running"), Password Hash Synchronization = Enabled (in Entra ID), successful domain join events in Windows VM Event Viewer (Event ID 4624)
  • Success: VMs can join domain successfully using credentials of user in AAD DC Administrators group, LDAP queries work from domain-joined VMs using LDAP://aaddscontoso.com, Group Policy applies to VMs after gpupdate /force, Health blade shows green status for all health checks

## 7. Subscriptions

### S - Simple Core
An Azure subscription is a billing container that groups resources together for cost tracking and has a credit limit or payment method attached - it's also the security boundary where RBAC roles and policies can be applied.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2023, Dropbox saved $75M over two years by restructuring their Azure subscriptions into dev/test/prod subscriptions with separate billing, enabling granular cost allocation per department and automated shutdown of dev resources after hours - their previous single-subscription model couldn't provide cost visibility and led to 40% waste from 24/7 dev VMs.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of subscriptions like separate bank accounts for different purposes: Just like you might have a checking account for daily expenses, savings for long-term goals, and a business account for company finances, Azure subscriptions separate workloads for billing, security, and governance. Your checking account (dev subscription) has a lower balance limit and looser spending rules, while your savings account (production subscription) has stricter controls and higher limits. Each account has its own statement (cost analysis), and you can't accidentally move money between them without explicit transfer (resource move).

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** Should you create separate subscriptions for development, test, and production environments, or use a single subscription with multiple resource groups?
**Answer:** Use separate subscriptions when you need isolated billing, different payment methods, or strict security boundaries (production data must not be accessible to dev team) - use resource groups within one subscription when environments share budget, security requirements, and admin team.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Subscriptions** with **Resource Groups**: Subscriptions are billing and administrative boundaries that contain multiple resource groups, while resource groups are logical containers for resources that share lifecycle and deployment - you can move resource groups between subscriptions, but subscriptions are top-level organizational units under a tenant.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Azure account (Microsoft Account or Work/School account), billing agreement (Pay-As-You-Go credit card, Enterprise Agreement, Cloud Solution Provider), or Azure Sponsorship/Credits (e.g., Visual Studio subscription includes $50-150/month credit)
  • Selection: Pay-As-You-Go (credit card, no commitment), Enterprise Agreement (EA - volume licensing for $$$K+ spend, requires contract), Microsoft Customer Agreement (MCA - online terms, invoice or credit card), Dev/Test subscriptions (discounted rates for non-production, requires EA or MCA)
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Subscriptions > Add (or Billing > Billing accounts > Create subscription if you're EA admin), or navigate to https://azure.microsoft.com/free for free trial subscription (200 USD credit for 30 days)

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Create subscription (EA): Azure Portal > Cost Management + Billing > Billing scopes > Select enrollment > Subscriptions > Add > Name = "Production-Workloads", Offer = Microsoft Azure Plan > Create
  • Set subscription quota limits: Subscriptions > Select subscription > Usage + quotas > View quotas for CPU cores (default 10 vCPUs per region), request increase via New support request if needed
  • Assign subscription administrator: Subscriptions > Select subscription > Access control (IAM) > Add role assignment > Owner role (full access) or Contributor (manage resources but not access)
  • Configure cost alerts: Subscription > Budgets > Add > Name = "Monthly Budget", Amount = $5000, Period = Monthly, Alert conditions = Actual cost 80% ($4000) and Forecasted 100% ($5000), Action group = Email finance team
  • Apply policy at subscription: Subscription > Policies > Assignments > Assign policy > Policy definition = "Allowed locations" > Parameters = East US, West US only (blocks resource creation in other regions)
  • Enable Azure Defender: Subscription > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > Select subscription > Enable Defender plans (Servers, Storage, SQL, etc.) - charges additional per-resource fees
  • Tag subscription for cost allocation: Subscriptions > Select subscription > Tags > Add tag: Department = Finance, CostCenter = CC-5678, Environment = Production (tags inherit to all resources for billing reports)
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** Subscription Owner can grant access to others AND manage all resources, Account Administrator (billing role) can create subscriptions and change billing but doesn't automatically get Owner role on created subscriptions - separate billing and access control responsibilities
  • **[Design Boundary]:** Maximum 50 subscriptions per Entra ID tenant for Pay-As-You-Go (can request increase to 200), unlimited subscriptions for Enterprise Agreement, most resource quotas are per-subscription per-region (e.g., 250 storage accounts per subscription per region), cannot merge subscriptions
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests understanding that subscriptions are billing boundaries, Owner role required to grant access but not required to create subscription (Account Admin/EA Admin creates), policies and tags at subscription level inherit to resource groups and resources, and moving resources between subscriptions requires Owner on both subscriptions

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Azure Portal > Subscriptions > Select subscription > Cost analysis blade (shows daily spending, forecast, breakdown by service/resource group), or Azure Monitor > Metrics for resource-level consumption
  • Metric: Month-to-date actual cost vs. budget amount, quota utilization percentage (Usage + quotas blade shows cores used / cores limit), number of policy violations (Policies > Compliance blade)
  • Success: Cost stays within budget threshold (no alert emails triggered), resource deployment succeeds without quota errors ("QuotaExceeded" error indicates need to request increase), policy compliance = 100% (zero non-compliant resources in Policies blade)

## 8. Management Groups

### S - Simple Core
Management Groups are containers that sit above subscriptions, letting you organize multiple subscriptions into a hierarchy and apply governance rules (policies, RBAC roles, budgets) once that automatically cascade down to all child subscriptions.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2022, a multinational bank with 240 Azure subscriptions across 15 countries used Management Groups to enforce GDPR compliance policies - they created a "Europe" management group that applied data residency policies (allowed-locations = EU regions only) to all 47 European subscriptions at once, saving 1,200 hours annually versus managing policies per subscription and preventing a potential €20M GDPR fine from accidental data transfer to US regions.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Management Groups like a corporate organizational chart: The root node (Tenant Root Group) is like the CEO, management groups are like divisions (Finance Division, Engineering Division), and subscriptions are like individual departments (Finance Accounting, Finance Audit). When the CEO sets a company-wide policy (all offices must use badge access), it automatically applies to all divisions and departments. The Finance Division head can add extra policies for their teams (all Finance employees need dual approval for purchases) without affecting Engineering, but they can't remove the CEO's badge policy. This hierarchy lets you govern at scale without touching each department individually.

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** When should you use Management Groups instead of applying policies directly to each subscription?
**Answer:** Use Management Groups when you have 3+ subscriptions that need to share governance rules (policies, RBAC, budgets) OR when you need to organize subscriptions by business unit/geography and apply different rules to each group - prevents duplicate policy assignments and ensures consistent governance as new subscriptions are added.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Management Groups** with **Resource Groups**: Management Groups organize subscriptions into a hierarchy for governance (policies, RBAC cascade down from parent to child subscriptions), while Resource Groups organize resources within a single subscription for deployment and lifecycle management - completely different levels of the hierarchy.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Management Group Contributor or Owner role on Tenant Root Group (or Global Administrator in Entra ID can elevate to gain access), understanding that all subscriptions initially under Tenant Root Group until you organize them
  • Selection: Flat structure (all subscriptions directly under Tenant Root Group) for small orgs, hierarchical structure (nested management groups like Geography > Business Unit > Environment) for enterprises, or sandbox structure (isolate dev/test under separate branch)
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Management groups > Start using management groups (first-time setup) > Create Tenant Root Group automatically > Add management group (or use PowerShell: `New-AzManagementGroup -GroupName 'Production'`)

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Create management group: Management groups > Add management group > Management group ID = mg-production (ID is immutable once set), Display name = Production Subscriptions, Parent group = Tenant Root Group > Create
  • Build hierarchy: Create child groups under mg-production: Create "mg-production-finance" and "mg-production-engineering" with Parent = mg-production (up to 6 levels deep from root supported)
  • Move subscriptions: Subscription > Overview > Management group > Change > Select destination management group (e.g., move subscription "Finance-Prod" from Tenant Root to mg-production-finance)
  • Assign policy at MG: Select management group > Policies > Assignments > Assign policy > Policy definition = "Require tag on resources", Tag name = CostCenter, Effect = Deny (prevents resource creation without tag), Scope = Current management group
  • Assign RBAC at MG: Management group > Access control (IAM) > Add role assignment > Role = Reader > Members = Finance-Audit-Group > Scope = Current management group (Finance auditors get read access to all subscriptions in this MG)
  • Configure budget at MG: Management group > Budgets > Add > Amount = $50,000/month, Scope = mg-production-finance (aggregates spending across all subscriptions in this MG and children)
  • Example hierarchy design:
    ```
    Tenant Root Group
    ├─ mg-production
    │  ├─ mg-production-finance (policies: PCI DSS compliance)
    │  │  ├─ Finance-Prod-Sub1
    │  │  └─ Finance-Prod-Sub2
    │  └─ mg-production-engineering
    │     └─ Engineering-Prod-Sub
    └─ mg-sandbox (policies: allowed-locations = dev regions only)
       └─ Dev-Test-Sub
    ```
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** Policies and RBAC assignments at Management Group level are inherited by all child management groups and subscriptions (cannot be blocked or removed at child level, except by policy exemptions), while tags are NOT inherited - you must apply tags at subscription/resource group/resource level
  • **[Design Boundary]:** Maximum 10,000 management groups per Entra ID tenant, maximum 6 levels of depth (excluding Tenant Root Group and subscription level), moving subscriptions between MGs takes up to 30 minutes to reflect in policy evaluation, root-level changes require elevated access
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests understanding that management group hierarchy depth is 6 levels, policies inherit downward (subscription policies can add but not remove MG policies), moving subscription to MG applies MG policies to subscription immediately, and Global Administrator must elevate access to manage Tenant Root Group

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Azure Portal > Management groups > Select MG > Policies > Compliance blade (shows policy compliance aggregated across all child subscriptions), or Azure Resource Graph for queries across MG hierarchy
  • Metric: Policy compliance percentage at MG level (target 100%), number of subscriptions under each MG (verify organizational structure), RBAC assignments inherited count (IAM > Role assignments > Show inherited)
  • Success: Policy compliance dashboard shows 100% compliant resources under management group, moving subscription to MG immediately reflects MG policies in subscription's Policies blade, budget alerts trigger when aggregated spending across MG subscriptions exceeds threshold

## 9. Resource Groups

### S - Simple Core
A resource group is a container that holds related Azure resources (VMs, storage accounts, networks) that you want to manage together as a single unit for deployment, updates, or deletion.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2021, an e-commerce company accidentally deleted their production database because it was in a resource group named "test-resources" with their dev VMs - proper resource group organization (production-database-rg with delete lock) would have prevented this $3.2M revenue loss incident during their Black Friday sale.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of resource groups like file folders on your computer: Just like you create a folder for a project (ProjectAlpha) containing related files (documents, spreadsheets, presentations), resource groups contain related Azure resources (web app, SQL database, storage account) for one application or workload. When you delete the folder, all files inside are deleted too (cascade delete). You can apply permissions to the folder level (read-only for collaborators) that apply to all files inside (RBAC inheritance). You wouldn't mix personal photos with work documents in the same folder - similarly, don't mix production and dev resources in the same resource group.

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** Should you create one resource group per application, per environment, or per resource type?
**Answer:** Create resource groups based on shared lifecycle - all resources that are deployed, updated, and deleted together should be in one group (e.g., web-app-production-rg contains web app + database + storage for production app), NOT by resource type (putting all VMs in one RG across different apps creates management chaos).

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **Resource Group deletion** with **Resource deletion**: Deleting a resource group permanently deletes ALL resources inside it (cascade delete, cannot be undone), while deleting an individual resource leaves the resource group and other resources intact - always double-check the resource group name before clicking delete.

**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Contributor or Owner role on subscription where you're creating the resource group, decision on resource group location (metadata stored in that region, but resources inside can be in different regions)
  • Selection: Naming convention (e.g., {app-name}-{environment}-rg like webapp-production-rg), organizational strategy (by application lifecycle, by department, by billing/cost center), location for resource group metadata (choose region for compliance or proximity to resources)
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Resource groups > Create > Subscription = Select subscription, Resource group name = webapp-production-rg, Region = East US (metadata location) > Review + create

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Create resource group: Resource groups > Create > Resource group = data-analytics-dev-rg, Region = West US 2 (only affects metadata, resources inside can be in any region) > Create
  • Apply tags for cost tracking: Select resource group > Tags > Add tags: Environment = Production, CostCenter = CC-1234, Owner = john@contoso.com (tags apply to billing reports, optional inherit to child resources)
  • Assign RBAC role: Resource group > Access control (IAM) > Add role assignment > Role = Contributor, Members = DevOps-Team (team can create/modify resources in this RG but not grant access) > Assign
  • Apply resource lock: Resource group > Locks > Add > Lock name = prevent-deletion, Lock type = Delete (allows modifications but blocks deletion) or ReadOnly (blocks modifications and deletion) > OK
  • Set policy at RG level: Resource group > Policies > Assignments > Assign policy > Policy = "Allowed virtual machine SKUs", Parameters = Standard_B2s, Standard_D2s_v3 only (blocks creation of expensive VM sizes)
  • Move resources between RGs: Source resource group > Select resource > Move > Move to another resource group > Destination RG = new-app-rg (requires downtime for some resources like VMs, validates dependencies)
  • Export ARM template: Resource group > Deployments > Select deployment > Template > Download (extracts JSON template of all resources in RG for redeployment)
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** Resource group location is where metadata is stored (for compliance - EU resource group stores metadata in EU), but resources inside can be in ANY Azure region - a resource group in East US can contain VMs in West Europe
  • **[Design Boundary]:** Resource groups cannot be nested (flat structure only), maximum 980 resource groups per subscription, resources can belong to only ONE resource group at a time (moving changes resource ID), deleting resource group is asynchronous (takes minutes to hours depending on resource count)
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests understanding that delete lock prevents resource group deletion but allows resource updates, tags on resource group do NOT automatically inherit to resources (must apply separately or via policy), moving resources between resource groups changes resource IDs (breaks ARM template references), and resources in RG can be in different regions than RG metadata location

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Azure Portal > Resource groups > Select RG > Overview blade (shows resource count, location, subscription, total cost), or Activity log (tracks all operations on RG and resources inside)
  • Metric: Total estimated monthly cost for all resources in RG (Cost analysis blade), resource count per type (e.g., 5 VMs, 2 storage accounts), lock status (Locks blade shows if delete or read-only lock applied)
  • Success: Resource group appears in list immediately after creation, tags show correctly in Cost analysis reports (allow 24 hours for billing data to populate), lock prevents deletion when testing (attempting to delete RG with delete lock returns error "Cannot delete resource group due to lock")

## 10. Azure Resource Manager (ARM) Templates

### S - Simple Core
ARM Templates are JSON files that define the infrastructure and configuration for your Azure resources as code, letting you deploy the same environment repeatedly and consistently instead of manually clicking through the portal each time.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2020, Maersk shipping company recovered from the NotPetya ransomware attack by using ARM Templates to rebuild 4,000 servers and 150 applications in Azure within 10 days - their templates automated identical production environment deployment across six regions, a process that would have taken 6 months manually and saved their $300M daily shipping revenue stream.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of ARM Templates like IKEA furniture instructions: The JSON template is the instruction manual with numbered steps (resources in deployment order), diagrams showing each part (parameters for customization like VM size), and hardware bag contents (variables for reusable values). Instead of describing to someone "build me a table," you hand them the IKEA instructions (template) and they can build identical tables (deploy identical environments) every time. Parameters are like choosing wood color (production vs. dev VM sizes), and the dependsOn sections ensure you attach legs before the tabletop (deploy VNet before VM).

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** When should you use ARM Templates instead of manually creating resources in the Portal?
**Answer:** Use ARM Templates when you need to deploy the same environment multiple times (dev, test, staging, prod), need version control for infrastructure (track changes in Git), require automated CI/CD deployments, or need to ensure consistent configuration across regions - never for one-off resource creation.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse **ARM Templates (declarative)** with **PowerShell scripts (imperative)**: ARM Templates declare the desired end state (what should exist), and Azure figures out how to create it (order, dependencies), while PowerShell scripts are step-by-step commands (do this, then do that) - templates are idempotent (run 10 times = same result), scripts are not.

---
**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**- PROVISION:**
  • Prerequisite: Understanding of JSON syntax, Azure resource types and properties (reference at docs.microsoft.com/azure/templates), text editor (Visual Studio Code with Azure Resource Manager Tools extension recommended for IntelliSense)
  • Selection: QuickStart template from Azure QuickStart Templates GitHub (800+ community templates), export existing resource as template (Portal > Resource > Export template), or create from scratch using VS Code
  • Execution: Azure Portal > Resource groups > Select RG > Deployments > Create > Build your own template in editor (or Azure CLI: `az deployment group create --template-file template.json --parameters parameters.json`)

**• CONFIGURE:**
  • Basic template structure (required sections):
    ```json
    {
      "$schema": "https://schema.management.azure.com/schemas/2019-04-01/deploymentTemplate.json#",
      "contentVersion": "1.0.0.0",
      "parameters": {},
      "variables": {},
      "resources": [],
      "outputs": {}
    }
    ```
  • Add parameters for customization:
    ```json
    "parameters": {
      "vmSize": {
        "type": "string",
        "defaultValue": "Standard_B2s",
        "allowedValues": ["Standard_B2s", "Standard_D2s_v3"],
        "metadata": {"description": "VM size for the virtual machine"}
      },
      "adminPassword": {
        "type": "securestring",
        "metadata": {"description": "Admin password for VM"}
      }
    }
    ```
  • Define resource with dependencies:
    ```json
    {
      "type": "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines",
      "apiVersion": "2023-03-01",
      "name": "[parameters('vmName')]",
      "location": "[resourceGroup().location]",
      "dependsOn": [
        "[resourceId('Microsoft.Network/networkInterfaces', variables('nicName'))]"
      ],
      "properties": {
        "hardwareProfile": {"vmSize": "[parameters('vmSize')]"},
        "osProfile": {
          "computerName": "[parameters('vmName')]",
          "adminUsername": "[parameters('adminUsername')]",
          "adminPassword": "[parameters('adminPassword')]"
        }
      }
    }
    ```
  • Use variables for reusable values: `"variables": {"nicName": "[concat(parameters('vmName'), '-nic')]"}` creates NIC name dynamically
  • Deploy template: Portal > Custom deployment > Build your own template > Load file template.json > Edit parameters (vmSize, adminPassword) > Review + create (validates template before deployment)
  • Linked templates for modularity: Reference external template URL in `"templateLink": {"uri": "https://storageaccount.blob.core.windows.net/templates/network.json"}` to break large deployments into reusable modules (network template, VM template)
  • Deployment modes: Complete mode (deletes resources in RG not in template - dangerous for existing RGs) vs. Incremental mode (default - only adds/updates, doesn't delete) - set via `"mode": "Complete"` in deployment
  • **[Critical Distinction]:** Parameters allow different values per deployment (dev vs. prod VM sizes), while Variables are computed once during deployment (cannot be overridden, used for complex expressions like concat() or reference() functions)
  • **[Design Boundary]:** Template size limited to 4 MB (use linked templates for larger deployments), maximum 256 parameters per template, deployment name limited to 64 characters, cannot conditionally depend on resources (dependsOn must always process, use condition property instead), deployment history limited to 800 operations per resource group
  • **[Exam Focus]:** AZ-104 tests understanding that dependsOn ensures deployment order (VNet before VM NIC), parameters.json file provides values at deployment time, resourceGroup().location function uses RG location for resources, outputs section exposes values like public IP for consumption by other templates, and Incremental mode is default safe deployment mode

**○ MONITOR:**
  • Tool: Azure Portal > Resource groups > Select RG > Deployments blade (shows deployment history, status, timestamp), click deployment name to see Inputs, Outputs, Template, Correlation ID
  • Metric: Deployment state (Succeeded, Failed, Running), duration (how long deployment took), error messages for failed deployments (click "Error details" for specific resource failure reason like QuotaExceeded)
  • Success: Deployment status = Succeeded (green checkmark), all resources appear in resource group with correct configuration matching template, outputs section displays expected values (e.g., VM public IP, storage account name), template validation passes before deployment starts (validates JSON syntax, required properties, API versions)

## 11. Azure Policy

### S - Simple Core
Azure Policy enforces rules across your Azure resources to maintain compliance standards—preventing unauthorized configurations before they happen.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2019, Capital One suffered a $80M breach penalty when misconfigured S3 buckets exposed 100M customer records; Azure Policy prevents similar disasters by automatically blocking resource deployments that violate security rules like "Storage accounts must use HTTPS only" or "VMs must use managed disks," catching violations before production deployment.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Azure Policy like building code enforcement: Azure Resource Manager is the construction site (deployment environment), Policy Definitions are the building codes (specific rules like "no asbestos," "fire exits required"), Policy Assignments are the inspectors assigned to neighborhoods (scopes like subscriptions or resource groups), and Compliance Reports are the violation notices (showing which buildings fail inspection).

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** When should you use Azure Policy instead of Azure RBAC to prevent a configuration issue?
**Answer:** Use Azure Policy when you need to enforce "what" configurations are allowed (e.g., "only Premium storage accounts"), not "who" can perform actions—RBAC controls permissions, Policy controls resource properties.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse Azure Policy with Azure Blueprints: Policy enforces individual configuration rules continuously (like "require tags"), while Blueprints package multiple policies, role assignments, and resource templates into repeatable environment deployments (like "deploy compliant landing zone").

---

**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**PROVISION:**
• Prerequisite: Contributor or Owner role on subscription, resource group, or management group scope where policy will be assigned
• Selection: Choose from 400+ built-in Policy Definitions (e.g., "Allowed virtual machine size SKUs," "Audit VMs without disaster recovery configured") or create Custom Policy Definition using JSON with Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines or Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts resource types
• Execution: Navigate to Azure Portal > Policy > Definitions > Select built-in policy or "+ Policy definition" > Define parameters like allowedLocations array ["eastus", "westus2"]

**CONFIGURE:**
• Create Policy Assignment by navigating to Policy > Assignments > Assign policy > Select scope (Management Group, Subscription, or Resource Group) and choose enforcement mode (Default or DoNotEnforce for testing)
• Define Assignment parameters—for "Allowed locations" policy, specify allowedLocations parameter with ["East US", "West US", "North Europe"] array to restrict deployment regions
• Set Policy Effect in definition JSON: Use "Deny" to block non-compliant deployments, "Audit" to log violations without blocking, "DeployIfNotExists" to auto-remediate (e.g., deploy Diagnostic Settings), "Append" to add required tags, or "Modify" to alter resource properties during deployment
• Configure Exclusions scope to exempt specific resource groups (e.g., /subscriptions/{sub-id}/resourceGroups/exempted-rg) from policy enforcement for sandbox environments
• Enable Managed Identity when using "DeployIfNotExists" or "Modify" effects—assign System-assigned identity with Contributor role to subscription scope for remediation tasks
• Create Initiative Definition (Policy Set) combining multiple policies—for example, "CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark v1.3.0" bundles 90+ policies for comprehensive compliance
• **[Critical Distinction]:** Policy evaluation occurs at resource creation (ARM template deployment), update, and during compliance scan cycles (every 24 hours by default); existing non-compliant resources require manual Remediation Task creation
• **[Design Boundary]:** Policy evaluation adds 2-5 second latency to ARM deployments; complex policies with nested conditions may exceed 20KB JSON size limit; use multiple simpler policies instead

**MONITOR:**
• Tool: Azure Policy Compliance Dashboard in Portal > Policy > Compliance showing percentage compliant by policy assignment
• Metric: Review Compliance State showing Compliant vs. Non-compliant resource count; filter by Resource Type (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines) or Policy Assignment name
• Trigger Remediation Task for "DeployIfNotExists" policies by selecting non-compliant policy > Create Remediation Task > choose Re-evaluate resource compliance before remediating
• Export compliance data using Azure Resource Graph queries: `PolicyResources | where type == 'microsoft.policyinsights/policystates' | where properties.complianceState == 'NonCompliant'`
• Success: 100% compliance rate on critical policies; zero "Deny" events blocking legitimate deployments; Remediation Tasks complete within SLA (typically 30 minutes for 1000 resources)

## 12. Resource Locks

### S - Simple Core
Resource Locks prevent accidental deletion or modification of critical Azure resources by adding a protective layer that even Owner-role users cannot bypass without first removing the lock.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2020, a global retailer's junior admin accidentally deleted their production SQL Database during a cleanup task, causing $2.1M in lost revenue during 8 hours of recovery from geo-replicated backup; a CanNotDelete lock would have prevented the delete command from executing, requiring explicit lock removal before resource deletion.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Resource Locks like safety locks on industrial equipment: The resource is the machine (VM, database, storage account), the Lock Type is the lockout mechanism (CanNotDelete is a padlock preventing removal, ReadOnly is a full lockout preventing operation and removal), Lock Inheritance is the cascade system (parent lock flows to child resources), and Lock Override is the supervisor key (only Owner can remove locks, requires two-step unlock-then-delete process).

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** You applied a ReadOnly lock at Resource Group level—which operations are blocked on resources inside that group?
**Answer:** ALL write operations are blocked including starting/stopping VMs, modifying configurations, adding resources, AND deleting resources; only read/list operations succeed—ReadOnly is more restrictive than CanNotDelete.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse Resource Lock scope with Azure RBAC inheritance: Locks inherit downward from parent scopes (subscription → resource group → resource) and block even Owner-role actions, while RBAC permissions inherit upward and can be overridden by higher-scope assignments.

---

**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**PROVISION:**
• Prerequisite: Owner or User Access Administrator role at scope where lock will be applied (subscription, resource group, or individual resource)
• Selection: Choose CanNotDelete lock type (prevents deletion but allows modifications) or ReadOnly lock type (prevents deletion AND any property changes including start/stop operations)
• Execution: Navigate to Azure Portal > Resource Group > Settings > Locks > + Add > Enter lock name "prod-database-lock" and select Lock type

**CONFIGURE:**
• Apply CanNotDelete lock at Resource Group level navigating to RG > Locks > Add lock > Type: Delete, Name: "prevent-accidental-deletion", Notes: "Contact DevOps lead before removing"
• Set ReadOnly lock on critical individual resources like Azure Portal > SQL Server > Locks > Add > Type: Read-only to prevent schema changes or configuration updates
• Configure lock via Azure CLI: `az lock create --name prodLock --lock-type CanNotDelete --resource-group myRG --notes "Production environment protection"`
• Create subscription-level lock using PowerShell: `New-AzResourceLock -LockLevel CanNotDelete -LockName "sub-level-lock" -Scope "/subscriptions/{subscription-id}"`
• Verify lock inheritance—child resources automatically inherit parent scope locks; explicitly check resource-level lock status with `az lock list --resource-group myRG --resource-name myVM --resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines`
• **[Critical Distinction]:** ReadOnly locks block Azure Automation runbooks, ARM template deployments, and Log Analytics agent configuration updates—use CanNotDelete for resources requiring operational changes
• **[Design Boundary]:** Lock operations appear as ARM write operations (Microsoft.Authorization/locks/write); locks do NOT prevent data plane operations like uploading blobs to storage or querying SQL databases, only control plane changes; removing locks requires separate unlock permission

**MONITOR:**
• Tool: Azure Activity Log filtered by Operation name "Microsoft.Authorization/locks/delete" to audit lock removal events
• Metric: Query Activity Log for failed operations with error "ScopeLocked" indicating blocked actions—count of blocked deletions per week validates lock effectiveness
• Review Lock inventory using Azure Resource Graph: `authorizationresources | where type == 'microsoft.authorization/locks' | project name, properties.level, resourceGroup`
• Alert on unauthorized lock removal by creating Activity Log alert rule: Alert condition = "Delete Lock (Microsoft.Authorization/locks)" with Action Group sending email to security team
• Success: Zero accidental resource deletions in production scopes; lock removal events correlate with approved change requests; ReadOnly locks don't block legitimate operational workflows

## 13. Cost Management and Budgets

### S - Simple Core
Azure Cost Management tracks spending across subscriptions and resource groups in real-time, while Budgets send automated alerts when costs approach defined thresholds—preventing surprise bills before month-end.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2021, Codecov faced a $100,000 unexpected Azure bill when a cryptocurrency mining attack exploited leaked credentials to spin up 500 GPU VMs across multiple regions; Cost Management anomaly detection flagged the 4000% spending increase within 6 hours, and budget alerts at 80% threshold ($20K) could have prevented $80K in fraudulent charges.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Cost Management like a business financial dashboard: Azure resources are expense line items (VM hours, storage GBs), Cost Analysis is the financial reports (breakdown by department/project), Budgets are spending guardrails (monthly limits with warning lights), Anomaly Detection is the fraud alert system (unusual spending patterns), and Recommendations are the cost accountant (suggesting Reserved Instances or rightsizing).

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** Your cost analysis shows 60% of monthly Azure spending is on stopped-but-not-deallocated VMs—what action reduces costs immediately without losing data?
**Answer:** Deallocate VMs using "Stop" in Azure Portal (not guest OS shutdown) to release compute charges while retaining disks; or configure Auto-Shutdown schedules for dev/test VMs to automatically deallocate during non-business hours.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse Azure Budget alerts with Azure Monitor metric alerts: Budget alerts trigger on accumulated spending thresholds ($5000/month) via Cost Management API, while metric alerts trigger on resource performance metrics (CPU > 80%) via Azure Monitor—use budgets for financial governance, metrics for operational health.

---

**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**PROVISION:**
• Prerequisite: Billing Reader role minimum for viewing costs; Cost Management Contributor role for creating budgets at subscription scope; EA enrollment admin for enterprise-wide cost views
• Selection: Choose scope for cost analysis—Management Group (all subscriptions), Subscription, Resource Group, or Tag-based view (e.g., all resources tagged Environment:Production)
• Execution: Navigate to Azure Portal > Cost Management + Billing > Cost Management > Cost analysis > Set scope and time range (Last 30 days, Current month, Custom date range)

**CONFIGURE:**
• Create Budget by navigating to Cost Management > Budgets > + Add > Set Amount ($10,000), Reset period (Monthly, Quarterly, Annual), Start/End dates
• Configure alert conditions at percentage thresholds: Alert at 50% ($5,000), 80% ($8,000), 90% ($9,000), and 100% ($10,000) of budget amount

• **[Critical Distinction]:** Budgets are notification-only mechanisms—they do NOT automatically stop resources or enforce spending limits; implement enforcement using Azure Policies (e.g., deny VM SKUs) or Automation runbooks triggered by alert webhooks

## 14. Tags

### S - Simple Core
Tags are name-value pair labels you attach to Azure resources (like "Environment:Production" or "CostCenter:HR") enabling organization, cost tracking, and bulk management of resources across subscriptions.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2018, a Fortune 500 manufacturer saved $3.2M annually after implementing comprehensive tagging strategy—by tagging 12,000 Azure resources with "Environment:Dev/Test", they identified $1.8M in abandoned development resources running 24/7, plus $1.4M saved by applying Azure Hybrid Benefit to correctly tagged Windows VMs.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Tags like library catalog cards: Resources are books (VMs, databases, storage accounts), Tag Names are catalog categories (Author, Genre, Year), Tag Values are the specific entries (Author:Tolkien, Genre:Fantasy), Tag Policies are cataloging rules (every book must have ISBN), and Tag-based Cost Reports are filtered book lists (show all Fantasy books published after 2000).

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** You need to automatically shut down all development VMs at 7 PM daily to save costs—how do tags enable this without hardcoding resource names?
**Answer:** Tag all dev VMs with "Environment:Dev", then create Azure Automation runbook using `Get-AzResource -TagName "Environment" -TagValue "Dev" | Where-Object {$_.ResourceType -eq "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines"}` to dynamically target VMs, ensuring newly created dev VMs are automatically included.

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse Tags with Resource Groups: Resource Groups are management containers (one resource belongs to exactly one RG, used for lifecycle and RBAC scope), while Tags are flexible metadata labels (one resource can have 50 tags, used for cross-RG organization and cost allocation)—use RGs for deployment boundaries, tags for business classification.

---

**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**PROVISION:**
• Prerequisite: Contributor or Tag Contributor role at scope where tags will be applied; Owner role required to enforce tagging via Azure Policy
• Selection: Define tag taxonomy with 5-10 standard tag names (Environment, CostCenter, Department, Owner, ApplicationName, DataClassification) and allowed values list (Environment: Dev|Test|Staging|Production)
• Execution: Navigate to Azure Portal > Resource > Tags > Add name-value pairs or bulk-apply tags via Resource Group > Tags > Apply to contained resources

**CONFIGURE:**
• Apply tags at resource creation using ARM template parameters: `"tags": {"Environment": "[parameters('environmentType')]", "CostCenter": "CC-1234", "Owner": "john.doe@company.com"}`
• Bulk tag existing resources using Azure CLI: `az resource tag --tags Environment=Production CostCenter=CC-5678 --ids $(az resource list --resource-group myRG --query "[].id" -o tsv)`
• Enforce required tags using Azure Policy "Require a tag and its value on resources"—configure policy parameter tagName:"Environment", tagValue:"Production|Development|Testing"
• Inherit tags from Resource Group using Azure Policy "Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing"—auto-applies RG tags to child resources during creation
• Create tag-based Cost views in Cost Management: Filter by Tag = "Department:Engineering" to show departmental spending; export monthly reports grouped by CostCenter tag for chargeback
• Implement tag naming convention: Use PascalCase or kebab-case consistently (CostCenter vs. cost-center), maximum 512 characters per tag value, avoid special characters except dash and underscore
• Automate tag compliance using Azure Resource Graph query: `resources | where tags !has "Environment" | project name, resourceGroup, type, tags` to find untagged resources
• **[Critical Distinction]:** Tags applied to Resource Group do NOT automatically flow to contained resources—use Azure Policy with "Inherit" effect or Automation scripts for cascading; tags on Subscription or Management Group scopes do NOT cascade at all
• **[Design Boundary]:** Each resource supports maximum 50 tags; tag names and values are case-insensitive for matching but case-preserving for display; tags do NOT replicate to resource metrics in Azure Monitor (use resource properties instead); legacy ASM (Classic) resources do not support tags

**MONITOR:**
• Tool: Azure Resource Graph Explorer running tag coverage queries: `resources | summarize count() by tostring(tags.Environment), type` to count resources per Environment tag value
• Metric: Track tag compliance percentage—target 95%+ of resources tagged with mandatory tags (Environment, CostCenter, Owner); alert when new resources deploy without required tags
• Review tag usage in Cost Management > Cost analysis > Group by: Tag to identify untagged resources (shown as "Untagged" or blank) consuming budget
• Audit tag changes via Activity Log: Filter Operation name contains "tags/write" showing who modified tags and when—detect unauthorized cost center reassignments
• Success: All production resources have complete tag sets; cost reports accurately allocate 98%+ of spending to business units via CostCenter tags; automated scripts successfully filter resources by Environment tag for lifecycle operations

## 15. Azure Storage Accounts

### S - Simple Core
Azure Storage Account is a container holding blobs, files, queues, and tables in Azure's cloud storage—providing scalable, secure, and globally accessible data storage with 11 nines (99.999999999%) durability.

### H - High-Stakes Example
In 2017, GitLab nearly lost 300GB of production database data when a misconfigured storage replication failed; switching from Locally Redundant Storage (LRS) to Geo-Redundant Storage (GRS) on Azure Storage provides automatic asynchronous replication to a secondary region 300+ miles away, protecting against regional disasters with 16 nines durability at only 2× cost.

### A - Analogical Model
Think of Storage Account like a bank branch building: The storage account is the branch facility (namespace contoso.blob.core.windows.net), Performance Tier is the service level (Standard = regular teller, Premium = private banking), Replication type is the vault backup strategy (LRS = on-site safe, GRS = copies at headquarters 300 miles away), Blob containers are safety deposit boxes (organizing stored items), and Access Keys are the branch master keys (full permissions to all boxes).

### P - Pattern Recognition
**Question:** You need to store 50TB of VM backup files accessed once per quarter for compliance—which storage account configuration minimizes cost?
**Answer:** Create StorageV2 (general-purpose v2) account with Standard performance tier, Locally Redundant Storage (LRS) replication, and Cool access tier—then move files to Archive tier after initial upload, reducing storage cost by 90% compared to Hot tier (~$0.002/GB vs. $0.018/GB per month).

### E - Elimination Logic
⚠️ Don't confuse Storage Account type with Access Tier: Account type (StorageV2, BlobStorage, FileStorage) determines supported services and features, while Access Tier (Hot, Cool, Archive) controls per-blob storage cost and retrieval latency within Blob Storage—you can have Cool-tier blobs in a StorageV2 account.

---

**LIFECYCLE DETAILS:**

**PROVISION:**
• Prerequisite: Contributor role on subscription or resource group; unique storage account name 3-24 lowercase letters/numbers (globally unique across Azure)
• Selection: Choose Storage account type—StorageV2 (general-purpose v2, recommended, supports all services and tiers), BlobStorage (blob-only, legacy), FileStorage (Premium files, NFS 4.1), BlockBlobStorage (Premium blobs, low latency)
• Execution: Navigate to Azure Portal > Create a resource > Storage account > Basics: Name "contosoprod001", Region "East US", Performance: Standard or Premium, Redundancy: LRS/GRS/ZRS/GZRS

**CONFIGURE:**
• Set Performance tier during creation—Standard (HDD-backed, supports Hot/Cool/Archive tiers, 20,000 IOPS per account) or Premium (SSD-backed, low latency < 10ms, 100,000+ IOPS, no tiering support, 3-5× cost)
• Select Replication strategy: LRS (3 copies in one datacenter, 99.999999999% durability), ZRS (3 copies across availability zones, withstands zone failure), GRS (6 copies, 3 local + 3 in paired region 300+ miles away, 99.99999999999999% durability), GZRS (combines ZRS and GRS for highest availability)
• Configure Networking: Enable Public endpoint (all networks) for testing, or select "Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses" > Add existing VNet subnets via Service Endpoints (Microsoft.Storage) or Private Endpoints (dedicated private IP in VNet)
• Enable Secure transfer required (HTTPS only) to enforce TLS 1.2 minimum—blocks unencrypted HTTP connections, recommended for compliance
• Set Minimum TLS version to "Version 1.2" in Configuration > Settings—rejects older TLS 1.0/1.1 clients vulnerable to POODLE and BEAST attacks
• Configure Access keys: Two 512-bit keys (key1, key2) for symmetric authentication; rotate keys using "Regenerate key1" without downtime by updating applications to key2 first
• Enable Blob versioning in Data management > Data protection to automatically maintain previous versions of blobs—protects against accidental deletion or overwrite, incurs storage cost for versions
• **[Critical Distinction]:** Premium performance tier requires selecting specialized account types—FileStorage for Premium file shares (SMB 3.0, 100,000 IOPS), BlockBlobStorage for Premium block blobs (low latency analytics), cannot convert between Standard and Premium post-creation
• **[Design Boundary]:** Maximum 250 storage accounts per subscription per region (soft limit, increasable); 500 TB maximum capacity for Standard accounts (5 PB for Premium); account name cannot be changed post-creation, requires data migration; LRS and ZRS do not protect against regional disasters
